## Proof

**Setup.** The integral is over $(0,1)^n$ with Lebesgue measure $\mu$, which is exactly the expectation $\mathbb{E}\!\left[\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^n X_j^2}{\sum_{j=1}^n X_j}\right]$, where $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are i.i.d. $\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ random variables.

Define
$$S_n=\sum_{j=1}^n X_j,\qquad Q_n=\sum_{j=1}^n X_j^2,\qquad R_n=\frac{Q_n}{S_n}.$$

**Step 1. Almost sure limit.** By the Strong Law of Large Numbers,
$$\frac{S_n}{n}\to \mathbb{E}[X_1]=\frac{1}{2}\quad\text{a.s.},\qquad \frac{Q_n}{n}\to \mathbb{E}[X_1^2]=\frac{1}{3}\quad\text{a.s.}$$

Since $S_n>0$ a.s. (each $X_j>0$ on $(0,1)$), we may form the ratio of these convergent sequences:
$$R_n=\frac{Q_n/n}{S_n/n}\;\longrightarrow\;\frac{1/3}{1/2}=\frac{2}{3}\quad\text{a.s.}$$

**Step 2. Uniform integrability / domination.** For every $x_j\in(0,1)$ we have $x_j^2\le x_j$, hence
$$0\;\le\; Q_n=\sum_{j=1}^n X_j^2\;\le\;\sum_{j=1}^n X_j=S_n,$$
so
$$0\;\le\; R_n=\frac{Q_n}{S_n}\;\le\; 1\quad\text{a.s. for all }n.$$

The constant $1$ is integrable on the probability space, so $\{R_n\}$ is uniformly bounded, hence uniformly integrable.

**Step 3. Exchange limit and expectation.** By the Dominated Convergence Theorem (applicable since $|R_n|\le 1$ a.s. for all $n$),
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[R_n]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lim_{n\to\infty}R_n\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{2}{3}\right]=\frac{2}{3}.$$

**Conclusion.**
$$\boxed{\lim_{n\to+\infty}\int_{(0,1)^n}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2}{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j}\,d\mu=\frac{2}{3}}.$$
